source: Polonius and I never spoke of it at the time, but...
Your apology means nothing, now that both you and she are dead.
And it wouldn't help anything. It was a long, long time ago.
I would understand if you no longer spoke to me.
No. I need you, and you need me.
You can make it up to me by helping me survive this.
Help me keep the people I love alive. That's how you can make this right.
In that case, I am at your service.
Nothing I could say could possible amend that crime.
So I will say nothing more.
Father—I want to talk about the way Mother died, and about the dockhouse where her belongings might be.
Ah. I'm sorry for that. It... was the sort of terrible news I had planned to tell you when you were older.
I see. So someone must have told you...
I'm... really quite sorry for that. It was the sort of terrible news I had planned to tell you when you were older.
Well, you're older now, and you deserve to know. As does your brother, when he returns.
Well, you're older now, and you deserve to know. As does Laertes.
I would never have wanted you to keep that from me. Even if it hurt to tell me. I deserved to know.
You're right. And yet... the heart works in strange ways, doesn't it? I told myself it was easier to bury it, to never speak of it.
As though if I did that, it wouldn't be true.
You told me some of her things are still in the dockhouse. Won't you help me see them?
Some of her things are still in the dockhouse. Won't you help me see them?
Aah... Ophelia, that house is still used sometimes to house victims of illness.
The last thing I need is to lose you. Going in there is incredibly dangerous.
My mother passed away alone in a plague quarantine—at King Hamlet's request. Her things are still there.
You never told me, my lady. Why?
I didn't feel it was my place to tell you, or your brother.
When they took your mother away, you were still nursing, and your brother clung to my skirts, crying. He was so young, he likely doesn't remember.
Before your mother was forced onto the boat, she asked me to keep you both safe, to see that you grew up well attended to.
And I always knew you would. Look at you. Beautiful, brave, and strong. Your mother, as I am, would be proud.
Thank you, my lady. I... don't know what to say. You've been very kind.
I just pray that your father tells Laertes. He deserves to know, too.
Can you help me get into the dockside shack where her belongings rest?
I'm afraid I can't.
You've never seen the town or castle ravaged by plague. When I was a girl, it was all too common here.
Hundreds would sicken and die in mere days. If any pestilence remains in that shack... it's a threat to us all.
Your mother would want you and Laertes safe, Ophelia. I know that above all.
Laertes... did you know about mother's death? Did you know what she left behind?
I knew she was ill. And then she passed. Father told me that.
My memory of her is... faint, at best...
Did father also tell you of her time spent in the sanitarium? That King Hamlet forced her into quarantine in the middle of nowhere before she died?
He... did that?
Cruel almost beyond belief. But of course, I'd expect nothing less of that man.
I never thought I'd say it, but I'm glad he's dead.
I always knew King Hamlet didn't like us. We always stood out to him.
We're not like them, Ophelia—the rest of the Danes, I mean—and we never will be. Don't forget that.
But long after they've given in to madness, or lovesickness, or fainting over themselves, you and I will still be here fighting.
Laertes. Some of mother's items are still in that shed on the docks.
I need you to help me retrieve them.
Aye. Let's go. We deserve to reclaim what's hers, Ophelia.
They can try to burn our family down at the roots, be ashamed of us, but we're still here, and we're not going anywhere.
I've learned how Mother died. It was inhuman. Some of her things are still in a shack near the docks.
Your mother? Lady Elise?
What of her?
Did you know? Did you know about her death?
I didn't. Your brother and I were... four years, perhaps five.
But it got worse. After she was sick, King Hamlet sent her to the sanitarium to die, alone and far from family.
She wasn't permitted to live out her days in the outer apartments, where the other plague victims go.
Bernardo, nobody ever told me. Were they... ashamed?
I'm so sorry. I've never... heard of the way Lady Elise met her end.
If I had known, rest assured, I would have told you.
Some of her personal items are still in a shack by the docks.
I need entry. But I'm not strong enough to break the door.
That old shack? But the King had Marcellus board it up a decade ago. It's possible plague still lingers inside.
To open it would present a grave danger to all living here now.
You're already in grave danger! From each other! What harm would it do?
I cannot disobey the King, Ophelia. You know that.
...So be it.
I'll find another way.
Your brother sent my mother to die alone in plague quarantine. Some of her personal items remain.
My brother sent her to the sanitarium, did he? I never knew.
I'm afraid I didn't pay very close attention to your mother at the end of her life. I was... otherwise occupied. My apologies.
Had I been King, she would have died a death fitting of her station, surrounded by her family.
Whether that's true or not...
There's nothing I can do about that at the moment. But her personal items are still locked up in that shack on the docks.
If you could only let me in there—
Into the plague shack? Are you insane?
No. I'll not have my men go anywhere close. We require that shack to be opened solely by sailors and the ill. Do you want to catch plague?
I'm terribly sorry about your mother, Ophelia. But I forbid you to go into that shack.
There's nothing I can do about that at the moment. I just thought you should know.
Your father sent my mother to die alone in plague quarantine. Some of her personal items remain.
My father did that?
You never heard about this from him?
No. I remember your mother's passing very little. All I can recall is that she was with us one week, and missing the next, and no one would speak of her.
Where are her personal items?
They're in the small dockhouse. You know the one. It's been boarded up for years. Can you help me get in?
Ah, but the plague...
Yes, it's possible we'd catch plague. But if you could only let me in there, I'd go in alone. You wouldn't need to come.
I... I want to, but...
As I recall, you were rather prone to taking ill when we were young. What if some pestilence still lingers in there?
I couldn't live with myself if that happened.
Hamlet, I want this more than anything.
You of all people. I thought I could come to you, at least.
Very well. I'll open it.
I'll meet you near the docks as soon as I'm able.
Find me there.
They're in the small dockhouse. You know the one. It was boarded up until recently.
I'll be fine, Hamlet. But I had to try to get in.
I've learned about my mother's death. King Hamlet sent her to die in a sanitarium along the southern coast, alone.
But why not simply let her heal up within the castle, just like the others?
You and I both know why. Because we'll always be outsiders within Denmark.
... Listen, my dear. I've a tale for you.
When I was a boy in Rome, my father and I often brought our spice wares to sale late at night and communed with the other traders before we passed the night there.
For a long time, we were the only Indian-born men to do so. Our colleagues thought us savage. We were allowed at no fires, given no drink. We drank alone, together.
And then... others came. Others like us. And we made our own fires. We told our own stories, stories about gods with names the Romans had never heard.
Eventually, we outnumbered the men who wouldn't let us drink with them, and they came to sit near our fires. They listened to our tales.
Someday all the places in the world like Denmark will be that Roman market.
And someday, you won't feel so alone, and neither will I.
Until that day, we make our own fire, and they kill us piece by piece before we are well and truly dead.
I'm sorry to hear about your mother. You are living proof that there can be a better way, Ophelia. You're loved by all.
...If I am loved, it is only for my father's blood.
I think you do yourself too little service.
Let's look out for one another. Let's keep our own fire.
Does Peter Quince seem a bit strange to you, my King?
Quince... that name is familiar. Ah. You mean that little traveling playmaster?
Oh, goodness, Lady Ophelia. The man's been coming to Elsinore for years. Always peculiar.
My wife sent for him this time. I've no idea why. Perhaps to cheer Hamlet's dour mood.
Does Peter Quince seem a bit strange to you?
Quince? I assume you mean that man who comes to perform at Elsinore now and then?
The Playmaster's job is to play the fool. If he was not strange, he would be a poor fool, would he not?
To tell you the truth, I've always found him a little off-putting, myself. That hinged smile! Those eerie eyes!
I wish the royal family weren't so enamoured with him, and his strange one-man 'acting troupe.'
My Queen, does Peter Quince seem... a bit strange to you?
I've always been fond of Quince, but I will admit his performances are... unique.
Every time he puts on a show, I laugh.
But then afterwards, thinking about the events they covered... I find myself strangely sad.
He has a funny way of finding humor in tragedy, and of hiding melancholy behind a smile.
I suppose that's why we keep inviting him back.
Quince, why is it that you know things you ought not to?
You are a simple one, aren't you.
You very well know the answer to that.
...Would you like to have a little peek behind the curtain?
To know how I cause such chaos?
...What do you mean by that?
So be off. Don't you have plans of your own to pursue?
You were so adamant earlier, after all!
I find it quite endearing, to be honest.
What's that, now? I merely observe what happens around me closely, looking for inspiration in every word.
